about.title: San Leandro Car Accident Claims
about.longDescription: Traffic through San Leandro moves in layers. I-880 carries the long-haul commute, Route 185 and E 14th Street run through the heart of town, and Washington Avenue ties the neighborhoods together. Those four corridors show up most often in public collision records for the city, and in 2025 San Leandro logged 304 injury collisions, 405 people hurt, and 3 traffic deaths. Reports cluster on Wednesdays between 5 and 7 p.m., when the evening drive is at its heaviest. If one of those crashes was yours, you probably have questions that feel bigger than the paperwork in front of you. Who covers the ER bill? What do you say when the other driver's insurer calls? How long do you have? LawProactive exists for that moment. We are not a law firm. We are a free service that connects you with an independent personal injury attorney who handles Alameda County car accident claims on contingency, so nothing is owed unless there is a recovery. You tell us what happened; we make the introduction.

whyChoose.title: Why San Leandro Drivers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: The clock in California is shorter than people expect
items.desc: Most car accident claims must be filed within two years, but a claim involving a city, county, or state agency may need to be presented within six months. An attorney can sort out which deadline applies to your crash before it passes.

items.title: Partial blame does not close the door
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, so you can still pursue compensation even if you were partly responsible for the collision. Your recovery is simply reduced by your share of fault rather than wiped out.

items.title: Free to connect, contingency to hire
items.desc: LawProactive never charges you, and the independent attorneys in our network work on contingency, meaning no fee unless they recover for you. California also places no cap on non-economic damages like pain and lost enjoyment of life in ordinary car accident cases.

items.question: The other driver's insurance adjuster wants a recorded statement. Should I give one?
items.answer: You are not required to give the other driver's insurer a recorded statement, and it is generally wise to decline until you have spoken with an attorney. Adjusters are trained to ask questions that can later be used to shrink or deny your claim. Politely take their contact information and let a lawyer handle the conversation.

items.question: My crash happened on I-880 in San Leandro during the evening commute. Does the freeway location change anything?
items.answer: Freeway collisions are usually handled by the California Highway Patrol rather than San Leandro police, so your report will come from a different agency. Multi-car pileups are also common in stop-and-go traffic, which can raise questions about how fault is shared among several drivers. Under California's pure comparative fault rule, an attorney can pursue each responsible party for their portion of the harm.

items.question: What should I be saving right now?
items.answer: Keep every photo from the scene, the exchange of insurance information, medical discharge papers, and receipts for anything you paid out of pocket. Write down the names of witnesses and note where the crash happened, whether that was E 14th Street, Washington Avenue, or elsewhere. Do not repair or dispose of your vehicle until your attorney says the damage has been documented.
